prompt: She couldn't buy groceries without strangers asking for a picture, and every restaurant she walked into went quiet as people reached for their phones.
He checked the clock every few minutes, rehearsed his opening line under his breath, and felt his palms go damp as the microphone was handed to him.
The whole class laughed when she stumbled over the word, and she wished the floor would open up and swallow her.
Everyone else was ordering another round, and when he said he had to be up early they groaned and told him not to be boring.
She had crossed eight time zones in a day, and now at three in the afternoon she could barely keep her eyes open.
He stared at the blank page for an hour, typed a sentence, deleted it, and went to make his fourth coffee.
The driver behind leaned on the horn, swerved around them, and shouted something through the window before roaring off.
Nothing that fell past that edge ever came back, not even light.
The glaciers had retreated a mile since her grandfather's photographs, and the summers now brought fires instead of rain.
Every photo was filtered, every caption was cheerful, and she scrolled for an hour feeling worse with each one.
He kept refreshing the page, watching the little number under his post tick upward, unable to put the phone down.
Her stomach growled, she had eaten nothing since breakfast, and the smell from the bakery was almost unbearable.
He had not slept in two days, the words on the screen swam, and he kept reading the same line over and over.
She counted the coins on the table twice, then put the milk back on the shelf.
The house was silent, the phone never rang, and he set the table for one again.
She kept the letter in her pocket all day and read it again on the train, smiling at nothing.
He checked her phone while she was in the shower and felt sick when he saw the name.
The kids ran between the tents in their pajamas while their parents argued about how to light the stove.
The fog rolled in, the horn sounded twice, and the passengers were told to return to their cabins.
She laced her shoes, pinned the number to her shirt, and joined the crowd shuffling toward the starting line.
He set the alarm for four, packed a thermos, and checked that the flies were still in the box.
The lights went down, the orchestra tuned, and the curtain shivered as someone moved behind it.
The room smelled of chalk and floor wax, and thirty small chairs faced a board covered in cursive letters.
The beeping never stopped, the sheets were stiff, and every few hours someone came to check the drip.
She scanned the rows of numbers, sighed, and moved another column into the red.
They dimmed the lights, the cake came out with more candles than anyone wanted to count, and the singing began.
The rings were exchanged, someone cried in the second row, and the photographer asked everyone to move closer.
Everyone wore black, spoke in low voices, and took turns standing beside the flowers to say a few words.
The tree was up, the stockings were hung, and the children were told to go to sleep or he wouldn't come.
The children ran from door to door in costumes, holding out bags and shouting the same two words.
The stands roared as the ball sailed over the fence and the man on second began to jog.
He lined up the white ball, chalked the tip, and sank the black in the corner pocket.
She moved the knight, glanced at the clock, and pressed the button before he had finished writing down his move.
The dealer slid two cards across the felt, and he pushed his last stack of chips into the middle.
The lights flickered, the water rose past the doorstep, and they carried the photographs upstairs.
The ground shook, the dishes rattled off the shelves, and everyone ran to stand in the doorway.
The sky turned green, the sirens started, and they hurried the children into the cellar.
The mask fogged, the regulator hissed, and the reef appeared below them in colors that did not exist on land.
She clipped into the rope, chalked her hands, and looked up at the overhang for the tenth time.
The snow squeaked under the boards, and he leaned into the turn as the trees blurred past.
The dough had doubled in size, and she punched it down and shaped it into a loaf.
The needles clicked, the ball of wool shrank, and the scarf grew an inch every evening.
He turned the soil, pressed the seeds in a finger deep, and watered the row until it darkened.
The jury filed back in, the room went quiet, and the foreman stood up with a folded piece of paper.
The suspect's story changed twice, the alibi did not hold, and the detective asked him to sit back down.
The cabin pressure changed, her ears popped, and the seatbelt sign came on with a chime.
The conductor punched her ticket, the fields slid past the window, and she fell asleep against the glass.
The waves lifted the board, she paddled hard, and for three seconds she was standing on water.
The telescope tracked the smudge of light as it crossed the constellation for the third night running.
The mice in the second group gained no weight at all, and the lab meeting ran an hour late.
